value.overview: The Great Black-backed Gull (Larus marinus) is the largest gull in the world. It is a powerful, broad-winged seabird of the North Atlantic, recognized by its very dark back and wings, white head and underparts, and large yellow bill. Adults are dominant predators and scavengers that take fish, marine invertebrates, eggs, young birds, carrion, and refuse. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to rare visitor rather than a regular resident or breeding species.
value.classification: The Great Black-backed Gull belongs to the order Charadriiformes and family Laridae, the gulls, terns, and skimmers. Its scientific name is Larus marinus.
value.identification: Adults are very large and heavy-bodied, with broad wings, a thick yellow bill often marked with a red spot, white head and underparts, pinkish legs, and a blackish back and wing tops. In flight, the broad wings and extensive white wing-tip markings are noticeable. Juveniles and immature birds are brown and heavily patterned, becoming progressively whiter and darker-backed over several years. Size, bulky shape, and very dark mantle help separate it from smaller dark-backed gulls.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds around rocky coasts, offshore islands, estuaries, salt marshes, and large northern lakes across the North Atlantic, including eastern Canada, the northeastern United States, Greenland, Iceland, and parts of northern and western Europe. It feeds and rests along ocean shorelines, beaches, harbors, tidal flats, fishing grounds, and estuaries. In Costa Rica it is not a regular breeding or resident species; it has been recorded as a rare, mainly coastal visitor, including on the Caribbean coast at Tortuguero.
value.migrationStatus: Northern populations migrate south after breeding, while many adults remain near breeding areas year-round. Costa Rica lies well south of the normal wintering range, so occurrences there are exceptional or very uncommon records, probably involving vagrants or occasional overshooting migrants rather than a predictable seasonal population.
value.breeding: Breeding usually begins at about four years of age. Pairs nest on coastal cliffs, rocky islands, dunes, marsh edges, or other open ground, often returning to the same territory. The nest is a shallow cup made from grasses, seaweed, moss, and other vegetation. Typically two or three eggs are laid, and both adults incubate them. Young hatch covered in down and are fed by both parents; they remain dependent for weeks after leaving the nest.
value.dietFeeding: The Great Black-backed Gull is an opportunistic omnivore and predator. It eats fish, crabs, mollusks, marine worms, carrion, discarded food, eggs, and young birds. It may steal food from other birds, capture seabirds, forage in intertidal zones, follow fishing vessels, or scavenge around harbors and landfills. Its large bill and strong body allow it to handle prey and food items that are unavailable to many smaller gulls.
value.behavior: This gull is assertive, intelligent, and often aggressive around food or nesting areas. It commonly rests in groups on beaches, rocks, mudflats, pilings, and rooftops, but adults defend territories during breeding. It swims readily and is a strong flier, using broad wingbeats and soaring over coastlines. Vocalizations include loud, harsh calls used in territorial defense, alarm, contact, and interactions between mates and young.

conservation.populationTrend: Global numbers have generally been stable or increasing over the long term, although trends differ among regions and some local breeding populations have declined.
